clue.text: One of those GI graffiti in bars?

definitions.text: One of those GI graffiti in bars?

parts.words: One of those GI graffiti in bars?
parts.note: a GI is an American soldier, a Yank, and graffiti are doodles; 'in bars' says it is a tune written in musical bars

explanation.surface: A question about scribbles left by American soldiers on the walls of pubs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bars' points to drinking places, but these are bars of music: a doodle drawn by a Yankee soldier becomes the old American marching song.
explanation.definitionFit: The well-known American patriotic song, whose title pairs a nickname for a US soldier with a word for an idle scribble.

clue.text: But would he have been heard to say it to Rose-red?

definitions.text: But would he have been heard to say it to Rose-red?

parts.words: But would he have been heard to say it to Rose-red?
parts.note: in the Wars of the Roses the red rose was Lancaster and the white was its rival house; a supporter of the white rose would hardly speak lovingly to a red-rose follower

explanation.surface: A question about whether a man would ever say something affectionate to a girl called Rose-red.
explanation.walkthrough: In the Wars of the Roses, Lancaster wore the red rose and the house of the white rose fought it; one of the white-rose side would never be heard to offer kisses to Rose-red.
explanation.definitionFit: A supporter of the white-rose royal house that fought Lancaster in the fifteenth-century Wars of the Roses.

clue.text: Sessions here 'lead to the furtherance of avian species

definitions.text: Sessions here 'lead to the furtherance of avian species

parts.words: Sessions here 'lead to the furtherance of avian species
parts.note: sessions are sittings, and birds sit on eggs in these places to hatch the next generation

explanation.surface: Meetings held somewhere that help bird conservation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sessions' suggests committee meetings, but here it means sittings: birds sit on their eggs and so further the species.
explanation.definitionFit: Structures birds build to lay and brood eggs, where sitting hatches the young.

clue.text: Expatiating on a photographic process

definitions.meaning: expatiating on a subject is speaking at length about it, expanding on it
making a bigger print from a negative

explanation.definitionFit: The word means expanding on a theme in speech, and making a bigger print in the darkroom.

clue.text: Irons in the fire

parts.note: the idiom means several projects on the go, but literally andirons are the metal stands that hold logs in a fireplace

explanation.surface: Having several projects under way at once.
explanation.walkthrough: The idiom suggests many schemes; literally it means firedogs, the iron supports for logs on a hearth.
explanation.definitionFit: Firedogs, the metal stands for logs in a hearth, are known by this short name.

clue.text: Umpire's decision approved without reservation

parts.note: out is the umpire's ruling against a batsman in cricket
right means correct, approved

explanation.surface: An umpire's call that was accepted unconditionally.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket the umpire's raised finger means OUT.
explanation.definitionFit: Done completely or unreservedly, with no holding back.

clue.text: Sound security man of human understanding

indicators.note: sound says the word for security is heard, not spelt, giving the philosopher's name

parts.note: a lock keeps a door secure

explanation.surface: A reliable security guard who is very sympathetic.
explanation.walkthrough: John Locke wrote An Essay Concerning Human Understanding (1689); 'Sound' looks like 'reliable' but signals the homophone.
explanation.definitionFit: The English philosopher wrote An Essay Concerning Human Understanding.

clue.text: Fellow takes one to add to a university degree in Canada

parts.note: a fellow is a man
one is the Roman numeral I
BA, Bachelor of Arts

explanation.surface: A man who adds a qualification to his degree.
explanation.walkthrough: The pieces run in clue order: MAN, I, TO, BA, with 'takes' and 'add to a' as joining words.
explanation.definitionFit: A prairie province of central Canada, so a place in that country.

clue.text: Tea-box's got the worm, say ?

indicators.note: say tells the solver the possessive of the tea-box word is heard, not spelt

parts.note: a caddy is a box for keeping tea

explanation.surface: A tea caddy has become infested with a worm.
explanation.walkthrough: A caddis worm is the larva of the caddis fly, used as fishing bait.
explanation.definitionFit: The caddis worm is the aquatic larva of the caddis fly, commonly called a worm.

clue.text: The glow that results from a dip

definitions.text: The glow that results from a dip

parts.words: The glow that results from a dip
parts.note: a dip is a candle made by dipping a wick into tallow; the old cheap kind used the pith of a marsh plant as its wick

explanation.surface: A healthy glow after a swim.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests the glow of skin after a bathe; a 'dip' is also a dipped tallow candle, and this one had a reed-pith wick.
explanation.definitionFit: A cheap candle made by dipping the pith of a marsh plant in tallow, giving a feeble light.

clue.text: Bella's organ-duettist

parts.note: an organ flute stop has a name that splits into two girls' names, so the girl wanted partners Bella in it

explanation.surface: A woman who plays organ duets alongside her friend Bella.
explanation.walkthrough: The clarabella is an organ stop; split it and one girl's name sits with Bella in the stop's name, a duet on the organ.
explanation.definitionFit: A girl's name that joins with Bella to spell an organ stop, so the two names share the organ.

clue.text: Put in net, sir, confound it !

indicators.note: to confound is to throw into confusion, so the letters of these two words are jumbled

explanation.surface: An exasperated footballer cursing as he finally scores.
explanation.walkthrough: 'confound it' reads as an oath but is the anagram signal: NET and SIR rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: To insert something is to place it within something else.

clue.text: Dancing Oriole

parts.note: the Baltimore oriole is popularly called this in America, and Stravinsky's ballet of the same name gives the dancing

explanation.surface: A songbird bobbing about.
explanation.walkthrough: The bright orange Baltimore oriole has this as a folk name, and 'Dancing' points to Stravinsky's ballet, so a dancing oriole is the ballet's title.
explanation.definitionFit: A popular American name for the orange Baltimore oriole, also the title of Stravinsky's ballet.

clue.text: Introverts go to bed

definitions.meaning: to introvert something is to turn it inwards, as a verb

explanation.definitionFit: The phrasal verb means both to fold or direct inwards and, informally, to retire for the night.

clue.text: Aired a flat among waterside vegetation ?

indicators.note: among puts the flat inside the waterside plant word

parts.note: reeds grow at the water's edge
taken as written

explanation.surface: A flat ventilated in a waterside reed bed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Aired' fits as inflated again with air; the 'a' before 'flat' is a joining word, not a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To inflate again is to fill with air once more.

clue.text: Hot cars one crashed racing in Rome

indicators.note: the hot cars are wrecked, so their letters with the added one are thrown into a new order

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: Stolen cars and a joyrider wrecked during a race in Rome.
explanation.walkthrough: 'crashed' rearranges HOTCARS plus I (one) into the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Horse-drawn two-wheeled vehicles were what raced in the Circus Maximus in ancient Rome.

clue.text: Plant to aid Ur upset about running water

indicators.note: about puts the jumbled letters round the stream word
upset jumbles the letters of the two words

parts.note: a beck is a northern English word for a stream

explanation.surface: A plant meant to help the ancient city of Ur, distressed about water.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' jumbles AID UR and 'about' sets those jumbled letters around a beck, the north-of-England word for a stream; the plant is the coneflower.
explanation.definitionFit: A coneflower, a North American daisy-like garden bloom such as black-eyed Susan.

clue.text: Watch for cannibal after salesman's discussed

indicators.note: after places the cannibal word behind the salesman word

parts.note: a rep is a sales representative
a cannibal is an eater of human flesh

explanation.surface: A watch chosen for a man-eater after a salesman talks it over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'discussed' supplies no letters: a loose touch in this old clue, hinting at something said again, as a repeater watch strikes again.
explanation.definitionFit: A watch that strikes the hours or quarters again when a spring is pressed.

clue.text: Reference to a kind of turn with horses that are runaways

parts.note: a U-turn, named after the letter U
gee or gee-gee is a childish word for a horse

explanation.surface: A note about a carriage turning with its horses as they bolt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gee-gee' is British nursery talk for a horse; a U-turn supplies the letter U.
explanation.definitionFit: Those who flee their homes for safety are people who have run away from danger.

clue.text: Softly, softly in anger causes little fret

indicators.note: in places the two soft letters inside the word for anger

parts.note: to rile is to anger
p, piano, is the musical direction for softly
p again for piano, softly

explanation.surface: Keeping calm when angry causes only minor worry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fret' means worry on the surface but here a ruffling of water; P (piano) twice goes into RILE.
explanation.definitionFit: A small wave ruffling the surface of water, a light fretting.

clue.text: His name in short has a drawback

definitions.text: His name in short has a drawback

parts.note: Ed is the short form of the man's name the clue is about

indicators.note: back says the word draw is turned round to read the other way

explanation.surface: A man whose abbreviated name carries a disadvantage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'drawback' reads as one noun but splits in two, with 'back' turning the first half round; the whole clue also describes the man, whose name is shortened to Ed.
explanation.definitionFit: A man's name, commonly shortened to Ed, that the whole clue describes.

clue.text: Extremely curly is Rover in the yellow leaf ?

parts.note: Rover is a stock name for a dog
Macbeth's 'fall'n into the sear, the yellow leaf': sear means withered

explanation.surface: A curly dog in autumn among the fallen leaves.
explanation.walkthrough: Macbeth speaks of 'the sear, the yellow leaf'; the leaf is also a book page, whose turned-down corner curls.
explanation.definitionFit: A turned-down corner of a book page, curled over like a dog's droopy flap.

clue.text: Like the boat of a beaky guitarist

definitions.text: Like the boat of a beaky guitarist

parts.words: Like the boat of a beaky guitarist
parts.note: in Edward Lear's nonsense poem the Owl and the Pussy-cat go to sea in a beautiful boat of this colour, and the owl sings to a small guitar

explanation.surface: A description of the vessel belonging to a big-nosed musician.
explanation.walkthrough: The beaky guitarist is Edward Lear's Owl, who 'sang to a small guitar' aboard a boat of this pale green colour.
explanation.definitionFit: The colour of the Owl and the Pussy-cat's boat in Lear's poem, a light yellowish green.

clue.text: Red idler is perhaps

definitions.meaning: reddish-brown, the colour of oxidised iron
someone idle loses practice and becomes stiff

explanation.definitionFit: The word describes a reddish-brown colour and someone stiff or out of practice from disuse.

clue.text: Very little sack for a brew

definitions.text: Very little sack for a brew

parts.words: Very little sack for a brew
parts.note: a tiny porous paper pouch of leaves dropped into a cup to make a hot drink

explanation.surface: A small bag used when brewing up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sack' and 'brew' suggest wine or beer, but the little sack holds leaves for a cup of tea.
explanation.definitionFit: A small porous pouch of leaves infused in hot water to make a cup of the drink.

clue.text: What of a boy for spooning ?

definitions.text: What of a boy for spooning

parts.words: What of a boy for spooning
parts.note: the Irish phrase 'a ... of a boy' means a fine lad, and the same word names a soup eaten with a spoon

explanation.surface: Asking what sort of lad is suited to courting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spooning' suggests old-fashioned courting, but it is eating with a spoon; 'a broth of a boy' is an Irish phrase for a fine young man.
explanation.definitionFit: A thin soup eaten with a spoon, and part of the Irish phrase for a spirited lad.

clue.text: Bell is one step up

definitions.meaning: a bell is sounded, the past participle of the verb for ringing

explanation.definitionFit: The word is the past participle of ring, said of a sounded bell, and a ladder's crossbar.

clue.text: The good old days are here

definitions.text: The good old days are here

parts.words: The good old days are here
parts.note: The Good Old Days was a long-running BBC television music-hall show recorded at the City Varieties theatre in this Yorkshire city

explanation.surface: A nostalgic claim that happy times have returned.
explanation.walkthrough: The Good Old Days was a BBC music-hall programme (1953 to 1983) staged at the City Varieties theatre in this northern English city.
explanation.definitionFit: The Yorkshire city where the BBC's Victorian music-hall show was staged for thirty years.

clue.text: Luggage by jet conveyance for some old body

parts.note: a trunk is a large travelling box
a hose is a pipe that conveys a jet of water

explanation.surface: Suitcases sent by jet carrying something for an elderly person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'jet' suggests an aircraft, but it is a jet of water carried by a hose; the answer is the puffed breeches worn by Tudor men.
explanation.definitionFit: Full breeches reaching the thighs, worn in the sixteenth century, were clothing for the lower body.

clue.text: Drawer of water ?

parts.note: a drawer of water would normally fetch it from a well, but here the drawer is one who draws charts of seas and rivers

explanation.surface: Someone who fetches water from a well.
explanation.walkthrough: The biblical 'drawers of water' carried it; this drawer makes maps and charts of seas and waterways.
explanation.definitionFit: A surveyor who charts seas, lakes and rivers, so draws maps of bodies of water.
